comments.author: @mikahundin
comments.text:
1. Jesse Lyu, the speaker, is demonstrating the Rabbit R1 device and its features in a live unboxing demo.
2. He highlights the device's color, which he says is not accurately represented in his previous demos on Discord.
3. The device has a new user interface (UI) that is designed to fit alongside the analog screw wheel. The screw wheel has a nice click sound and resistance to it.
4. The device has numerous settings, including network settings for both serial and Wi-Fi connections.
5. Jesse demonstrates the device's ability to provide real-time information, such as the current weather in Los Angeles, using its 4G LTE connection.
6. He also shows how the new UI fits into the R1 phone factor, making it simple to scroll through information and return to the homepage.
7. Jesse mentions that they have worked hard on both the hardware and software to make the R1 the fastest and smartest device on the market.
8. He demonstrates the device's advanced reasoning capabilities by asking it who won the 2011 Formula 1 driver championship and who designed the winning car.
9. Jesse credits the new voice of the Rabbit, which was developed in collaboration with 11 Labs, as one of the device's standout features.
10. He also demonstrates the device's AI vision capabilities, which can identify objects and people in real-time.
11. Jesse mentions that they have made numerous improvements to the device over the past few months and that they are constantly learning and improving in the new AI domain.
12. He concludes by saying that the R1 is the fastest device on the market and that it has improved a lot in terms of its AI capabilities.

comments.author: @consciouscode8150
comments.text:
The comments on this video are missing the point so hard it makes me sad. As someone with severe executive dysfunction, using an app for every little interaction uses up spoons. You have to remember to do it in the first place, which app to use, how to use it, where to go in the GUI (because every single one is bespoke), etc and all those little things add up until I'm exhausted by decision fatigue. As a result, I typically don't even bother - I only use it for discrete actions I need in the moment. Even neurotypical people struggle with getting distracted by social media updates, notifications, news, etc.

To those saying "someone will make an app in 6 months" first, no they won't. Apps are sandboxed by the OS, they can't talk to each other except through the interfaces they explicitly expose. You would need OS-level integration like Bixby or Google Assistant with effectively root access, and even then they were never built to talk to each other. How long do I have to wait for Google to build a shitty walled garden and get developers to reimplement their APIs or do virtual GUI manipulation, if that's even possible in the Android ecosystem? Second, even with OS-level integration the silo app model severely limits what it's even capable of. This is a case of "in CS, it can be hard to explain the difference between the easy and the virtually impossible" (XKCD 1425).

With this, the OS was built from the ground up to interface between everything with the agent as the interconnect. I can tell it to redirect sound between apps or to external speakers, use it as a remote for devices which have none, set up some task automation, set up accounts on other devices, go through my email to filter out the 900 items I've procrastinated deleting. It's like the difference between telephone operators and the virtual switchboards. I've been waiting for something like this for years, because it could actually allow me to approach the productivity of someone who doesn't struggle with this. Easily worth $200. The humane pin was garbage from its inception, but this is an incremental improvement which is genuinely useful. It doesn't have to be a giant leap like the iPhone to be worthwhile.
